sections.h2: Does Nebraska have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?
sections.html:
Nebraska does not publish a separate capital gains schedule. The Department of Revenue's rate chronology lists one set of four bracket rates for individuals, and a gain from a house sale that is not excluded is taxed through that same schedule on the Nebraska return.

For tax year 2026 the top bracket rate is 4.55%, down from 5.20% in 2025. That is a real change for anyone closing a sale this year, because the old figure is still quoted on many websites.

Two layers matter when you sell a Nebraska house: the federal rules that decide how much of your gain is taxable, and the Nebraska bracket rates that apply to whatever is left on your state return. A third layer, the documentary stamp tax, is a transfer charge and not an income tax, so it is covered separately below.

sections.h2: What are the Nebraska income tax brackets for 2026?
sections.html:
For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, Nebraska uses four brackets with rates of 2.46%, 3.51%, 4.55% and 4.55%. The Department of Revenue sets the bracket limits by filing status.

BracketRate (2026)SingleMarried filing jointly
12.46%$0 to $4,130$0 to $8,250
23.51%$4,130 to $24,760$8,250 to $49,530
34.55%$24,760 to $39,900$49,530 to $79,800
44.55%Over $39,900Over $79,800

The 2026 standard deduction is listed at $8,850 for single filers and $17,700 for joint filers. The 2025 brackets were different, with a 5.01% third bracket and a 5.20% top bracket, so a sale that closes in December 2025 and one that closes in January 2026 land on different schedules.

The Nebraska tax rate chronology keeps the full history if you need an earlier year.

sections.h2: How much of the gain on my Nebraska home is tax free under federal law?
sections.html:
If the house was your main home, you may be able to exclude up to $250,000 of gain from federal income, or up to $500,000 on a joint return with your spouse. The IRS describes this in Topic 701 and Publication 523.

To qualify you must meet an ownership test and a use test. You meet the ownership test if you owned the home at least 24 months in the five years before the sale, and the use test if you lived in it as your residence at least 24 months in those five years. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months.

  • On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both spouses must meet the use test.
  • You generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home sale during the two years before this one.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence community members on qualified extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year period for up to 10 years.

Gain above the exclusion is the part that reaches your return, and that is where both the federal and Nebraska rates apply.

sections.h2: What federal rates apply to gain above the exclusion?
sections.html:
For most sellers who held the house longer than one year, the federal rate on net capital gain is 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on taxable income. The IRS lists the 2025 thresholds in Topic 409, and 2026 thresholds are adjusted each year.

Filing status (tax year 2025)0% up to15% up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

Income above the 15% limit is taxed at 20%. A gain on a house held one year or less is short-term and is taxed as ordinary income. Part of a gain tied to depreciation you took on a rental can be taxed at up to 25%, according to the same IRS page. Individuals with significant investment income may also owe the net investment income tax, which the IRS covers in Topic 559.

A loss on a personal home is not deductible. If you sell below what you paid, the IRS says the loss on personal-use property cannot be claimed.

sections.h2: What if I own a Nebraska house but live in another state?
sections.html:
A nonresident who sells Nebraska real estate files a Nebraska return for that gain. The Department of Revenue's residency guide says nonresidents pay Nebraska income tax on income from Nebraska sources, including income, gain, loss and deduction tied to owning or selling an interest in real property located in Nebraska.

This catches several kinds of sellers:

  • An owner who moved away and kept the house as a rental before selling.
  • Heirs living out of state who inherit a Nebraska house and sell it.
  • A former resident who left Nebraska mid-year and sold the house in the same year, who may be a partial-year resident.

Nonresidents report on Form 1040N, and the state also has a Nonresident Income Tax Agreement form. If you are in any of these groups, confirm filing status with the Department of Revenue or a tax professional before the closing date, since the gain can arrive in a year when you have no other Nebraska income.

sections.h2: How is gain figured if I inherited the Nebraska house?
sections.html:
Gain is the sale price minus your adjusted basis, and for an inherited house the basis follows special rules rather than the price the decedent paid. The IRS points to Publication 551 for property received by gift or inheritance, and Topic 703 explains that basis can be raised by improvements.

Whether an heir has any gain depends on that basis figure, so keep documentation of the house's value at the date of death. An appraisal, estate inventory or county assessment record can all help support the number.

Inherited property can also trigger Nebraska inheritance tax, which is a separate tax from income tax and is charged to the person receiving the property. Our Nebraska estate and inheritance tax guide covers the classes and rates.

sections.h2: What does the documentary stamp tax cost when a Nebraska deed is recorded?
sections.html:
The seller, as grantor, pays a documentary stamp tax when the deed is recorded. As of July 18, 2026, the rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000, up from $2.32 before that date, according to the Department of Revenue.

As an illustration only, a deed conveying property valued at $200,000 would carry $664 in stamp tax at the new rate (200 units at $3.32). The tax is collected by the county register of deeds.

The register will not record the deed without a completed Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, which the buyer or the buyer's agent files under Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-214. Some transfers are exempt, and the state's exemption list includes:

  • Deeds between spouses, or between parent and child, without actual consideration.
  • Deeds of distribution from a personal representative to heirs or devisees.
  • Transfer on death deeds.
  • Deeds given in lieu of foreclosure to secure or release a debt.

A normal arm's-length sale does not fall into these categories, so plan for the stamp tax in your closing numbers.

sections.h2: What do I report to the IRS after I sell?
sections.html:
If you receive a Form 1099-S, you must report the sale even when the whole gain is excludable. You also report it if you cannot exclude all of the gain. The IRS directs sellers to Form 8949 and Schedule D for the reporting.

A taxable gain can also require estimated tax payments during the year, which the IRS covers in Publication 505. Selling in the spring and waiting until April of the next year to settle up can leave you with an underpayment issue, so ask your preparer about a payment before year end.

If you sold under an installment contract, where part of the price arrives in later years, the IRS says you generally report under the installment method unless you elect out, and the home sale exclusion stays available.

sections.h2: A short checklist for Nebraska sellers thinking about tax
sections.html:
• Write down the purchase date, purchase price and every improvement receipt you can find.
  • Count whether you lived in the house for 24 of the last 60 months.
  • Note the 2026 versus 2025 Nebraska rate difference if your closing date is near year end.
  • Check whether any beneficiary or out-of-state owner needs a Nebraska return.
  • Add the $3.32 per $1,000 stamp tax to your closing estimate for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026.
  • Keep the 1099-S and settlement statement together for your preparer.

This page gives general information from official sources and is not tax advice. A Nebraska CPA or enrolled agent can run your actual numbers.

faqs.q: What is the Nebraska capital gains tax rate for 2026?
faqs.a: Nebraska has no separate capital gains rate. Gain that is not excluded is taxed through the individual brackets, which for 2026 are 2.46%, 3.51%, 4.55% and 4.55%, according to the Department of Revenue.

faqs.q: Do I owe Nebraska tax if I sell my main home?
faqs.a: Only if gain remains after the federal exclusion of up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return. Gain inside the exclusion is left out of income, but you still report the sale if you get a Form 1099-S.

faqs.q: How long must I live in the house to use the exclusion?
faqs.a: You need to have owned it and lived in it for at least 24 months each within the five years before the sale. The two 24-month periods do not have to overlap exactly.

faqs.q: Does Nebraska tax a nonresident who sells a house in the state?
faqs.a: Yes. The Department of Revenue says nonresidents pay Nebraska tax on income and gain connected with real property located in Nebraska, filed on Form 1040N.

faqs.q: Who pays the Nebraska documentary stamp tax?
faqs.a: The grantor, meaning the seller, pays it when the deed is recorded with the register of deeds. The rate is $3.32 per $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026.

faqs.q: Is inherited property taxed differently when sold?
faqs.a: The basis is set by special rules for inherited property, which the IRS explains in Publication 551. Nebraska may also charge inheritance tax to the heir, which is separate from income tax.
